brief.logline: The only ten minutes of a parent's morning nobody interrupts: each day one child toes a tape line with news that can't wait, until the last drop leaves the Solace dripper and out it comes.
brief.premise: In a kitchen mid-breakfast, a parent of three works through the only ten minutes of the morning nobody interrupts: kettle, grind, a slow hand pour into a Solace dripper, one cup. Masking tape crosses the floor, laid over an older strip worn gray. Nobody explains it. Each episode opens as the kettle goes down and the coffee starts to drain: one child reaches the tape with news that can't wait and stops, toes on the line. First the youngest, fist clenched around something. Then the eldest, holding out a permission slip and an uncapped pen at arm's length. Then the middle child, a hand pressed flat to their forehead. The parent clocks each of them and watches the dripper. From the tape the child sees the dripper, never the cup; we see the last drops fall. On the last drop the parent lifts the dripper off the cup, and the news comes out: the fist opens on a tooth; the slip gets signed against the fridge, cup never set down. In the finale, the hand comes down from the forehead on bangs the child has cut themself, and the parent takes a long first sip before saying anything at all.

content.format_rationale: Social series, because the idea runs on a situation that repeats with a new variable: the same pour and the same tape line, with a different child holding different news each time. That is one child at a time, the way the brand's own words say 'one cup at a time'. Seeing it again is what proves it happens every morning, without a voiceover saying so, and each episode pays off in 30 s with the sound off. Runner-up: a single 45 s ad spot. It lost because one morning reads as a one-off story. Lucas's line is about a routine, and the rule only reads as a rule the second time we see it.

what_makes_it_specific: Kept: 'The ten minutes of making coffee by hand are the only part of a parent's morning nobody interrupts.' The logline opens on that line, and every episode takes place inside those ten minutes.
Obvious version: a frazzled parent in a noisy kitchen finds calm over a hand pour while the kids' chaos blurs in the background, then smiles into the first sip.

Differs by who, and by what it costs them: the calm is not the parent's escape but a truce the kids keep. They stand at the tape holding a lost tooth, an unsigned slip or home-cut bangs, and they pay for the parent's ten minutes by staying quiet.

Product role: the dripper is the clock. The viewer's cue is its last drop and the child's cue is its lift, and a coffee machine would give nobody a reason to stand still. Swap in any other cone dripper and the clock still runs, so the brand's own words carry the difference. 'Glazed by hand, one cup at a time' is the rhythm of the series: one child, one piece of news, one cup, one morning. The end frame puts those exact words under the dripper, so each episode reads as the phrase acted out.

Added detail: the tape is re-laid over an older strip worn gray, and nobody ever explains it. The rule reads as years old without a word (taste notes: restraint over explanation; one real detail only this family has).

Taste, followed and broken on purpose: episodes 1 and 2 show the child as a fist, a pen and a slip (hands before faces). Episode 3 breaks that note because the bangs are the joke; A15 is the fallback. Scene sound only, no music. The product is a tool from the first second and a hero only on the end frame.
Alternative (not briefed): one morning the kids make the pour for the parent. That is a new central situation, so it is not developed here.

evidence.specificity: All six previous notes were addressed. Each episode now has a concrete object, action and payoff that casting, design and strategy can break down without asking: "First the youngest, fist clenched around something. The same goes for "the fist opens on a tooth; the slip gets signed against the fridge, cup never set down." The strategist gets an audience defined by situation and a signal that exists where the piece runs: "Signal: link taps per episode on the paid social placement, compared across episodes." The timing is now pinned in every label: "the youngest's toes reach the tape by 2 s". It stops short of 9 because one tone line is still loose ("Morning light falls as it actually does") and the tone entry 'Held' has a small conflict with the 2 s arrival (see notes).
evidence.distinctiveness: The change from the obvious version is in who and in what it costs them, not in tone: "the calm is not the parent's escape but a truce the kids keep. They stand at the tape holding a lost tooth, an unsigned slip or home-cut bangs, and they pay for the parent's ten minutes by staying quiet." The detail nobody asked for belongs to this family alone: "the tape is re-laid over an older strip worn gray, and nobody ever explains it." The Product role fix was made as asked: "'Glazed by hand, one cup at a time' is the rhythm of the series: one child, one piece of news, one cup, one morning." It is not a 9 because the brief itself admits "Swap in any other cone dripper and the clock still runs". The Solace difference is carried by the structure and the end-frame words, not by anything handmade we see on screen.

The end frame uses verified words only and adds no claim under either reading of A02: "'Solace. Glazed by hand, one cup at a time. $38.'" The story keeps the line true, because the kids wait instead of interrupting. The brief never paraphrases 'one cup at a time', never claims brew time, taste or durability, and "story_seed.turn" now reads "On the last drop the parent lifts the dripper off the cup, and the news comes out." It stays at 8 rather than 9 for the same reason as distinctiveness: 'glazed by hand' is said, never seen.

normalized_brief.logline: The only ten minutes of a parent's morning nobody interrupts: each day one child toes a tape line with news that can't wait, until the last drop leaves the Solace dripper and out it comes.
normalized_brief.premise: In a kitchen mid-breakfast, a parent of three works through the only ten minutes of the morning nobody interrupts: kettle, grind, a slow hand pour into a Solace dripper, one cup. Masking tape crosses the floor, laid over an older strip worn gray. Nobody explains it. Each episode opens as the kettle goes down and the coffee starts to drain: one child reaches the tape with news that can't wait and stops, toes on the line. First the youngest, fist clenched around something. Then the eldest, holding out a permission slip and an uncapped pen at arm's length. Then the middle child, a hand pressed flat to their forehead. The parent clocks each of them and watches the dripper. From the tape the child sees the dripper, never the cup; we see the last drops fall. On the last drop the parent lifts the dripper off the cup, and the news comes out: the fist opens on a tooth; the slip gets signed against the fridge, cup never set down. In the finale, the hand comes down from the forehead on bangs the child has cut themself, and the parent takes a long first sip before saying anything at all.

content.audience_tension: Who: parents who make coffee on a machine at home before school drop-off. The moment is mid-breakfast, while each kid brings them something that needs an answer before they leave. This is the recommended primary buyer. It narrows A05, and the choice goes to Lucas (see blockers). Proxy media can buy (assumption): paid social audiences of parents of school-age children with an interest in home coffee or coffee machines. In their voice: I want to hear their news the second it happens, yet I want one stretch of the morning when nobody needs me, and I'd hate to admit I'd rather they waited. [H1] What they'd hate to admit is that wanting those minutes makes them a less present parent. The cost isn't time. Take the product away and the conflict is still there: the tension never mentions coffee.
content.desired_behavior: Goal: parents who watch an episode tap through to the Solace dripper product page, where the $38 dripper is sold. That the sale happens on this page is an assumption: F1 gives the price, not the channel. The series turns repeat viewing into revenue. The same rule plays three times (D01-D03), so every episode is another chance at the product page, and D04 retargets episode viewers who didn't tap. H6 tests whether the sequence earns its cost. From (machine users, pending Lucas's buyer decision): makes coffee on a machine that brews while they answer the kids, and scrolls past pour-over as gear for people with quiet mornings (H4). To: taps the link on D01 and lands on the Solace dripper product page. Jobs: D01, 9:16 paid feed, full-screen, sound on but must read muted: opens the series and sets up the rule. Every paid path starts here; the ask is the tap. D02, same placement: the second sighting makes the tape read as a rule; the ask is the tap. content.product_relevance: Moment: a school morning, mid-breakfast. The parent stands at the counter pouring water through the dripper as a child arrives needing an answer. Without it: coffee from a machine makes itself in the background, the parent's hands are free, and every request lands mid-cup (H3). Fix: F1 "a ceramic pour-over dripper". The water goes through by hand (a category meaning, see assumptions), so the parent is visibly busy until the cup is made. The cup the news waits on comes through Solace's dripper, not a machine. That switch of method is the change this buyer makes, and it is argued here, not in proof. F2 "one cup at a time" matches the moment's rhythm, one cup to one child's news, if A02 reads it as brewing. Whether the pour ends on a moment the child can see is Blocked (proof point 3). No verified fact says how long a pour takes, so the moment must never suggest a duration. Barrier: to a machine user, pour-over looks like a hobby for people with quiet mornings, not a tool for a parent with three kids in the kitchen (H4). A second barrier the series can't answer: pour-over needs a kettle and filters as well as the dripper (H8). Permission: F2 "glazed by hand". A viewer can check this only if the product page says so. Beyond that, permission is not established. The moment works with no logo and no price because it is the pour itself, not the brand.

hypotheses: H1 Riskiest: parents who make coffee on a machine before drop-off want one stretch of the morning when nobody needs them, and would hate to admit they'd rather the kids waited. This is the tension. Test: 8 interviews with such parents, each walking through their last school morning. This first section never mentions coffee or guilt. Owner: strategy. Kills it if: fewer than 4 of 8 raise, unprompted, unease about wanting part of the morning to themselves.

H2: Lucas's insight that making coffee by hand is the part of a parent's morning that gets interrupted least. 'Ten minutes' and 'only' are unproven. If Lucas keeps machine users, it is the promise the series makes to them, so it is checked with parents who already make coffee by hand. If he picks hand-pour parents, it becomes their own recognition. Test: 8 interviews with parents who hand-pour before drop-off, asking which part of the morning gets interrupted least. Owner: strategy. Kills it if: fewer than 5 of 8 name making coffee. The spine then goes back to Lucas.

H3: a hand pour keeps the parent visibly busy where a machine leaves their hands free, and with the sound off this reads as the reason the child waits. The machine half is category knowledge; the test checks the half the work depends on. Test: the pre-flight gate, which shows the D01 rough cut muted to 8 primary-audience parents and asks what the child is waiting for. Owner: strategy with director. Kills it if: fewer than 6 of 8 name the coffee, the pour or the dripper, unprompted, as what the child is waiting for.

H4: for machine users, the main barrier is that pour-over looks like a hobby for quiet mornings, not the price. Test: in the H1 interviews, after the section without coffee, ask why they don't make coffee by hand, without offering reasons. Owner: strategy. Kills it if: fewer than 4 of 8 name fuss or 'not for mornings like mine' unprompted. If price leads instead, Rejected H-R2 comes back.

H8: machine users also hold back because pour-over needs kit they don't own, such as a kettle, filters and perhaps a grinder, on top of the dripper. The series can't answer this; the product page would have to. Test: the same question as H4, in the same interviews. Owner: strategy. Kills it if: fewer than 4 of 8 name extra kit unprompted. If it survives, see the kit blocker.

H5: no rival pour-over dripper brand or single-serve coffee machine leads with 'one cup at a time' or with a family waiting on the pour. Category knowledge, unchecked, says single-serve machines also sell one cup. Test: an ad-library scan of paid social from the main pour-over dripper brands and single-serve machines over the last 12 months. Owner: strategy (not run; no research tool bound). Kills it if: any rival leads with either. Then ask Solace for a verified fact only it can claim. Until then, Solace's own words and the execution carry the difference.

H6: repetition is what makes the rule readable (development's series rationale). Test: serve D02 cold to a holdout audience and compare it with D02 served after D01. Owner: media. Kills it if: D02 after D01 fails to beat D02 cold by the success criterion's margin (10% relative on sessions per 1,000 impressions, or the client's replacement figure). Rejected H-R1. In their voice: my coffee is the one thing I do for myself, yet I rush it like everything else. Rejected because it restates time and convenience as the loss, and it fails the remove-the-product test. Revive if: the H1 interviews describe morning coffee as rushed rather than guarded.

Rejected because 'pour by hand' is category language any dripper brand could sign, and it leaves out Solace's own words. Revive if: A02 comes back as glazing. assumptions: Market and language: North America, English (A16, based on the $ price).

Who has to act differently: new buyers. Recommended primary buyer: parents who make coffee on a machine (drip or single-serve) before school drop-off. The decision is Lucas's (see blockers), and the routes proceed on this buyer unless he picks otherwise. Why recommended: they are the only group for whom the 'Without it' line is true, and development's product role argues against the machine ('a coffee machine would give nobody a reason to stand still'). They change method, not just brand, so H4 and H8 cover the barriers. Parents who already pour by hand will see the series, but no From is built for them. Switch to them (development A05 if_wrong) if H1 dies among machine users, or if H8 survives and Solace can't answer the kit question on the product page. No base of existing owners was supplied.

Buyable proxy: paid social audiences of parents of school-age children with an interest in home coffee or coffee machines. Untested; media to confirm reach, and to confirm whether machine owners can be targeted apart from people who already pour by hand.

'One cup at a time' in the proposition quotes F2 word for word, so the paraphrase ban in must_avoid is kept.
'Keeps' means the news waits without spoiling, so the wait costs the family nothing. This resolves the tension's guilt. The proposition is for strategy only and never appears on screen (A01, A10).
'Pour-over' meaning the parent pours the water by hand is a category definition, not F1's own words. Only product_relevance uses it; the proposition and proof points do not depend on it.

Left out of proof: '$38' argues price and 'glazed by hand' argues craft, which are separate ideas. Both stay on the end frame per A10. 'Not a machine' argues switching method, so it sits in product_relevance, not in proof.
Studio threshold for H6 and its success criterion: a 10% relative lift. It is a pass mark set before the flight, not a claim or a benchmark, and the client may replace it.
Objective, audience and key_message are the client's wishes, not evidence.

Test design: H1, H4 and H8 share one set of 8 interviews with machine-using parents, and the section without coffee comes first. H2 uses 8 parents who already pour by hand. H3 and the pre-flight gate are one test with one pass mark: the D01 rough cut, muted, 8 parents, 6 of 8 naming the coffee, the pour or the dripper as what the child is waiting for.
Taste: the strategy follows 'restraint over explanation'. No taste note is broken at the strategy stage. The taste notes are marked as example notes, not Lucas's own.

content.recommendation_rationale:
'Their news keeps, one cup at a time' plays at 20-27.5 s: eyes come up only after the lift, and the tooth still lands in your palm as news. The 0-2 s glance puts the child's toes on the re-laid tape in frame before the cone can pass for a pour-over routine video, which machine users scroll past as gear for quiet mornings (H4). Success: the muted pre-flight gate, where 6 of 8 parents name the coffee as what the child waits for. The full 30 s D01 serves it, because the glance shows the parent has seen the child before the hold.
Gives up: the premise's 'we see the last drops fall'. R3 reads the drawdown as a water line from above, where R1 shows drops falling into a clear glass. It also splits parent and child across a cut where R1 holds them in one frame, and it never shows the parent's face.
Failure: 2-20 s. At phone size the drawdown seen from above can look like a still brown circle, and the toes at 20-30% of frame shrink to a strip of sock. Fix: cut to the cone while the water is still high, so the sinking line visibly travels, and keep white socks against the tape. The glance has already shown the toes large, so in the hold they only need to stay present. Never move the tape toward the kettle to make it bigger.
Kill test: in the muted pre-flight gate, parents read the POV as a parent ignoring a child: fewer than 6 of 8 name the coffee as what the child waits for, or they describe the wait as neglect even after the glance. Then first person has turned the guilt onto the viewer instead of dissolving it. Switch to R1, where both are in one frame and the rule reads as the family's, not yours.
Case R1: A12's phone test (A03). If the drops in R1's clear glass read muted at phone size and R3's water line from above doesn't, R1 is the pick.
Case R2: proof point 3 / A03 and A17 (Blocked). If A12's phone test shows the drawdown doesn't read from any angle, R2 is the pick, because its cue is the dripper leaving the cup as seen from the tape.

assumptions: [changed] Reviewer notes applied. R3 now opens on the glance and spends the tone's one allowed cut there. R1 and R2 each gain a beat only their own idea explains: in R1 the fist checks its news mid-hold; in R2 a toe presses the tape's lifting corner flat. Product jobs are restated by who reads the dripper: the viewer in R1, the child in R2, the parent in R3. Each route has one safe-band composition rule. 'Gives up', 'Case R1' and R3's 'Keeps' are rebuilt on what R1 keeps and R3 drops. R3's island depth, the direction of its hand-off and its pendant key are fixed. R3's rival swap is now a gate on the sample blocker. No note conflicted with the brief, the facts or another note.

The category's three most familiar ads (category knowledge, unchecked; no research tool bound): (1) the me-time ritual: a slow pour, steam, window light, a solo sip; (2) the pour-over routine or gear video: gooseneck spiral, bloom macro, scale readout, often shot POV; (3) the frazzled parent drinking coffee as fuel in the middle of kitchen chaos. R1 avoids 1 and 3 (a still kitchen, a pour shared with a waiting child). R2 inverts 3 (the kid holds the line and there is no chaos). R3 borrows 2's point of view but opens on a child's toes, so it never plays as one.

Ten one-liners were drafted and the three furthest apart kept. Dropped: 'pour-over makes a quiet morning' (sells the barrier by staging chaos, which drifts toward ad 3); 'kids time their news to the lift like showmen' (too close to R2); 'split screen joined on the lift' (a device, not a reframe); 'machine morning vs dripper morning' (implies a behavior claim and doubles the cast); 'the worn tape as years of mornings' (needs time jumps, reads sentimental); 'the dripper as the family queue' (turns on A02); 'the kids pour for the parent' (development already ruled this a new situation).

Buyer: the routes follow strategy's default of machine users until Lucas decides. R3's H4 argument applies to machine users only: the child is in frame before the cone can read as the routine video they scroll past. If Lucas picks parents who already pour by hand, R3 still works but loses that argument.

Questions for Lucas on what each route drops from the seed: R3 drops the visible last drops (read as a water line from above) and the parent's face (A11's on-camera parent becomes hands). R2 drops 'we see the last drops fall'. R1 swaps the mug under the dripper for a clear glass. R1 and R3 show the parent as hands and forearms. R2 lets the parent in soft, face turned down to the dripper, never the subject.

Safe band (a working assumption; media to confirm per platform): on the 9:16 paid placement, the account header covers roughly the top 15% and the caption and link button cover roughly the bottom 35%. That leaves about 15-65% of frame height. The 4:5 center crop keeps about 15-85% of a 9:16 frame. Every route puts the tape, the worn strip, the toes and the draining dripper inside 15-65%, so all four survive both the placement and D04.

Faces and camera height: the youngest's head sits at about the height of a dripper on a counter. Keeping the child's face out of D01-D02 therefore depends on where the camera is. R1 puts the lens above dripper height with the dripper nearer than the child. R2 shoots from behind the child. R3 frames the parent's glance below the child's chest. Production to confirm in the A12 test; blocking stays with later departments.

Tags: every P beat assumes A11's live shoot in one real kitchen. No shoot budget is authorized, so every P beat is an assumption. The C fallback builds each episode from its S02 cover still plus stills of the lift and the reveal, cut to scene sound. That keeps the story but fails the rule that something visibly changes by 1.5 s, so A11 works as a gate. No child is ever generated. G is kept for adult hands, water and kitchen plates only, and product shots stay live, per A11's if_wrong.

No product render or physical sample was supplied, so the glaze color, the outline, and whether drops show beneath the dripper are all unknown. No hex is given for the glaze, and every product close-up waits for the physical dripper.

Last drop: in an opaque mug the drop falls out of sight. R1 uses a clear glass so the drops and the rising level read with the sound off. R3 reads the drawdown from above (the water line and the bed). R2 uses the lift alone, seen as the outline leaving the island's edge. All three depend on A12.

Claims guard, all routes: no scale with a timer display, no wall clock and no steam macro in frame (these would imply brew time or heat). The D03 sip is a pause with a neutral face, never a taste verdict. Nothing refers to each glaze being unique, and 'ten minutes' never appears on screen. The kettle, grinder, scale and mug carry no visible brand marks.

Kettle safety (A08): the island is at least 90 cm deep, and production measures it against the youngest's reach. The kettle goes down on the parent's near edge. In R1 and R2 the child stays on the tape. In R3 the child comes no nearer than the island's far edge, and only after the lift. In R3's hand-off the parent's palm crosses the island to the child, and the child never reaches in. No scissors appear on screen; the bangs are already cut.
R3's POV borrows the grammar of creator routine videos. It runs as a branded Solace ad with no creator handle, username or first-person caption, so no one poses as a real customer.

Casting: the parent is any gender, cast as the seed's parent of three and not the 'mom needs coffee' type from ad 3. R1 and R3 need only the parent's hands and forearms, which also cuts continuity cost.

Taste notes (example notes, not Lucas's own). Followed: sound design before music, restraint over explanation, tool then hero, one real detail (the re-laid tape), and hands before faces. Broken on purpose: every route shows the child's face in D03 because the bangs are the joke (A15 fallback: a cut lock of hair in the hand). R2 also lets the parent's face in, soft and turned down to the dripper, because from a child's height the parent stands above it. R3's POV rig is a formal device inside the 'Real' tone; locking it off keeps it honest. R3 keeps the child's face out of the glance and the eyes-up frame until D03, so the finale is the first time 'your eyes' reach a face.
End-frame text is A10 as given: 'Solace. Glazed by hand, one cup at a time. $38.' The price waits on Lucas's A10 answer. Nothing else on screen quotes or paraphrases 'one cup at a time' (A02).

evidence.specificity: Checked: all six previous notes were addressed, and nothing was lost in fixing them. A writer, casting and production design can break R3 down without calling back. Its beats name the action, the object and the sound: "0-2 s [P, risky: a hand and the kettle; fallback: a hand double on a locked take, product stays live]: the glance. Your hand sets the kettle down on your side of the island (click)." Then "eyes down. The water line sits high in the cone, then sinks into the bed, and the bed flattens. At the top of the safe band the toes stay put. Your hands rest flat on either side of the mug. You don't look up again." The unpicked routes are just as concrete: R1 has "9-12 s is the beat only this route has: the fist loosens one knuckle, checks, and clenches again. Nobody else moves." Each hex color is tied to an object in frame ("#8A857C the worn strip under it"). The key, the Kelvin, the ratio and the sound source are named for every route. It stops at 8, not 9, because of one open question for design: which frame serves S02 (see notes).
evidence.distinctiveness: The pairing problem from the last round is fixed. Each route now has a beat only its own idea explains: R1's fist check, and R2's "a corner of the new tape has lifted. A sock toe presses it flat, presses again, then settles back behind the line." The product jobs split by who reads the dripper: the viewer in R1, the child in R2, the parent in R3. The admission that a rival dripper works just as well is now a gate: "the hold is built on one visible feature of the physical dripper that shows it was glazed by hand (F2)... It is shown, never called one of a kind. If the sample has no such feature, the brand rests on A10's words alone." The pick has a detail nobody else would think of: "The mug rises into frame for a long first sip, with the bangs over the rim." This is not higher because R3's central idea, "Answering mid-pour gets them a glance; finishing the cup gets them your eyes", names neither the dripper nor its lift. Of the three central ideas it is the only one that could headline any dripper brand's campaign word for word.

The rationale quotes the proposition at its beat: "'Their news keeps, one cup at a time' plays at 20-27.5 s: eyes come up only after the lift, and the tooth still lands in your palm as news." What R3 drops from the seed goes to Lucas as a question, as the brief requires: "Drops (questions for Lucas): the visible last drops, which read as the water line from above instead, and the parent's face (A11's on-camera parent becomes hands)." The must-avoids hold. The kettle is out of the child's reach: "the island is at least 90 cm deep... The kettle goes down on the parent's near edge, and the child never comes nearer than the far edge." The claims guard covers everything the facts don't: "no scale with a timer display, no wall clock and no steam macro." No mug appears in an end frame, and on-screen text is A10 only. The H4 sentence now argues for R3 instead of against it. Fit drops slightly in one place: the Tags line allows generated hands and water, which A11 does not (note 4).
evidence.craft: Both physical contradictions from the last round are gone. The narrowing fix is dropped. "your palm crosses the island to the child; the child never reaches in". The key is motivated by something the set has: "Key: the pendant over the island, top-down into the cone, 3500K; window fill frame right, 5600K; 2:1 (a school morning before sunrise)." Gives up and Case R1 are rebuilt on what R1 really has, and the Cases are tied to separate outcomes of one brief field: "Case R1: A12's phone test (A03). If the drops in R1's clear glass read muted at phone size and R3's water line from above doesn't, R1 is the pick." Failure is timed and has a fix that stays inside the tone's one cut. notes.note: Two problems. First, 'finishing the cup gets them your eyes' can be read as 'after you've drunk it'. That contradicts the seed: the news comes out on the lift, and in D03 the sip comes after the reveal. Second, of the three central ideas it is the only one with no Solace element, and most departments see only this sentence. Put the premise's turn into it. For example: 'Answer mid-pour and they get a glance; lift the dripper first and they get your eyes.' That is 17 words. It keeps the belief it costs (that answering at once is being present), makes the product's action the hinge, and matches the recurring device, so downstream departments build the lift as the moment.
